fields.title: Proverbs
fields.subtitle: Mishlei, “Proverbs”
fields.description: The Bible’s book of everyday wisdom, which begins with its motto — “Knowledge begins with the fear of the LORD” — and then brings that fear down to earth: words that calm anger and words that wound, the lazy one and the ant, honest scales and justice for the poor, friends who stay closer than a brother, and plans that only the LORD can make stand. A father teaching his son, Wisdom calling in the street and delighting beside God at creation, two houses and two invitations, the sayings of Solomon copied in Hezekiah’s day, Agur’s riddles, and the capable wife who closes the book. Thirty-one chapters, a chapter a day for a month, set out line by line as the poetry it is, in the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Proverbs?
qa.answer: A book of the Old Testament made of wise sayings and teaching poems about how to live well under God. Its Hebrew name, Mishlei, is its first word, “the proverbs of”; a mashal is a saying that teaches by comparison. Chapters 1–9 are long poems in which a parent instructs a son and Wisdom calls out in the streets; chapters 10–29 gather hundreds of short sayings, most of them two balanced lines; and chapters 30–31 hold the words of Agur, the words of King Lemuel and the poem of the capable wife. With Job and Ecclesiastes it is one of the wisdom books of the Bible.

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Proverbs?
qa.answer: Proverbs is a collection, and its headings name several sources. It opens with “the proverbs of Solomon”, the king remembered for speaking three thousand proverbs (1 Kings 4:32), and two large collections bear his name (10:1–22:16 and chapters 25–29). The second was “collected and copied by the officials of Hezekiah, king of Judah” (25:1), around 700 BC. The book also gathers “sayings of the wise” (22:17; 24:23), the words of Agur son of Jakeh (chapter 30) and of King Lemuel, taught by his mother (31:1). Scholars differ over how much goes back to Solomon himself and when the book took its final form, but it was clearly gathered over centuries.

qa.question: What does “the fear of the LORD” mean in Proverbs?
qa.answer: It is the motto of the book: “Knowledge begins with the fear of the LORD” (1:7), repeated at 9:10 and echoed in the last chapter, where the woman who fears the LORD “is the one to be praised” (31:30). It does not mean terror that runs from God, but reverent awe that trusts him and turns from evil. Proverbs defines it directly — “To fear the LORD is to hate evil” (8:13) — and describes it as trusting the LORD with your whole heart rather than relying on your own insight (3:5–7). In Proverbs, wisdom is skill in living, and it begins with knowing who God is.

qa.question: Are the sayings in Proverbs promises?
qa.answer: Not in the sense of guarantees. A proverb states how life usually goes in God’s world, compressed into a memorable line, and it has to be applied with judgment. “Start children off on the way they should go” (22:6) is wise and generally true, but it does not promise that every child of faithful parents will believe. Proverbs shows this itself by setting side by side “Do not answer fools on the terms of their folly” and “Answer fools as their folly deserves” (26:4–5): both are right, in different moments. The books of Job and Ecclesiastes, which stand beside Proverbs, take up the hard cases in which the righteous suffer and the wicked prosper.

qa.question: Who is the woman of Proverbs 31?
qa.answer: Proverbs 31:10–31 is an alphabetic poem, each of its twenty-two verses beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, in praise of “a capable wife” (in Hebrew eshet hayil, a woman of strength and worth, the phrase used of Ruth in Ruth 3:11). She works, trades, buys land, cares for her household and opens her hand to the poor, and she is praised because she fears the LORD. Many read her as the portrait of a real and admirable woman, and the poem is sung in Jewish homes on the eve of the Sabbath; many also notice that she embodies the Wisdom described in chapters 1–9, so that the book ends with wisdom lived out in a home. The chapter opens with the words King Lemuel’s mother taught him (31:1–9).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Each line of the poetry is set on its own, and “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Knowledge begins with the fear of the LORD, but fools treat wisdom and discipline with contempt.

— Proverbs 1:7

Some books of the Bible take you up a mountain or into the throne room of heaven. Proverbs takes you into the kitchen, the marketplace, the field at harvest time and the gate where the elders sit. It has things to say about how you talk, how you work, how you spend your money and how long you stay in bed. It is the most down-to-earth book in Scripture, and that is exactly the point. The God who made the heavens with wisdom wants that same wisdom to shape an ordinary Tuesday.

The book is made of short sayings and longer poems gathered over several centuries, most of them in two lines that balance each other like the pans of a scale. They are easy to remember and hard to forget. And because the book has thirty-one chapters, readers have long taken it a chapter a day through the month, as this library invites you to do with its Proverbs in a Month plan.

“Proverbs”

The Hebrew name of the book, Mishlei, is its first word: “the proverbs of”. A mashal is a saying that teaches by comparison, setting one thing beside another so that each throws light on the other. The word stretches wide: a two-line saying, a long teaching poem, a riddle, even a taunt.

The book opens by naming Solomon, “David’s son, king of Israel”. The account of his reign remembers that God gave him wisdom “as vast as the sand on the seashore”, and that “He spoke 3,000 proverbs, and his songs numbered 1,005” (1 Kings 4:29, 32). Proverbs does not claim that all its sayings are his, as the next section shows. But it places the whole collection under the name of the king who became, for Israel, what wisdom looked like.

A book of collections

Read the headings and you can see the seams. Proverbs is an anthology, put together in stages, and it tells you so:

  • A father’s instruction and Wisdom’s call (chapters 1–9): long poems in which a parent speaks to a son, and Wisdom herself calls out in the streets.
  • “The proverbs of Solomon” (10:1–22:16): several hundred two-line sayings, most of them standing on their own.
  • The sayings of the wise (22:17–24:22): introduced with “Bend your ear and hear what the wise have said”, and described as “thirty sayings”.
  • More sayings of the wise (24:23–34), ending with the field of the lazy man.
  • Proverbs of Solomon copied in Hezekiah’s day (chapters 25–29), “collected and copied by the officials of Hezekiah, king of Judah”, some two centuries after Solomon.
  • The words of Agur (chapter 30), full of riddles and numbered lists.
  • The words of King Lemuel (31:1–9), “an oracle that his mother taught him”.
  • The capable wife (31:10–31), an alphabetic poem that closes the book.

Two things stand out. First, the book was still growing in the time of Hezekiah, around 700 BC, and it gathered wisdom from beyond Solomon’s court: Agur and Lemuel are otherwise unknown and may not have been Israelites at all. The “thirty sayings” of 22:17–24:22 have long been compared with an Egyptian book of instruction, the Teaching of Amenemope, which is also arranged in thirty chapters and shares some of the same advice. Israel’s sages listened to the nations, and set what they heard under the fear of the LORD.

Second, the long poems of chapters 1–9 come first for a reason. They are the door into the book, and they tell you how to read everything after them.

The fear of the LORD

The opening verses say what the book is for: “for learning wisdom and discipline, for grasping words of insight”, for “making the naive shrewd”, and even for the wise, who will “gain still more learning”. Then comes the sentence at the head of this introduction, the motto of the whole book. Knowledge begins with the fear of the LORD.

The same words return at the end of the opening poems, “Wisdom starts with the fear of the LORD” (9:10), and again in the book’s last poem, where the woman who fears the LORD “is the one to be praised” (31:30). Proverbs is framed by them.

This fear is not terror that runs from God. It is the awe that comes from knowing who he is, and it shows itself in trust and in turning from evil. Proverbs defines it plainly: “To fear the LORD is to hate evil” (8:13). And its best-known lines describe it as a whole-hearted trust:

Trust the LORD with your whole heart, and do not rely on your own insight. Keep him in mind in everything you do, and he will clear a straight road ahead of you.

— Proverbs 3:5–6

That is why the wisdom of Proverbs is never merely cleverness. It is skill in living, the ability “to steer their way”, as 1:5 puts it, through a world that has a grain to it because God made it.

“My son”

Chapters 1–9 are spoken by a parent. “My son, listen when your father corrects you, and do not let go of what your mother teaches you” (1:8). Again and again the voice returns with the same words, “My son”, and once it remembers being taught in turn: “When I was a boy in my father’s house”, he says, his own father told him, “Hold on to my words with all your heart; keep my commands and you will live” (4:3–4). Wisdom is handed down, from one generation to the next, like a family inheritance.

The son addressed in these poems is a young man about to make his way in the world, and the dangers set before him are a young man’s dangers: a gang that promises easy money (1:10–19), and a woman who is not his wife (chapters 5–7). But the book has always been read by daughters as well as sons, and its last chapter puts a woman at the centre.

His great picture is of two roads. One is the road of the wicked, which looks inviting at the start and ends in the dark. The other is described in one of the loveliest sayings in the book:

But the road the righteous walk is like the light at daybreak, shining brighter and brighter until it is broad day.

— Proverbs 4:18

A few verses later comes the advice on which the whole road depends: “More than anything you protect, protect your heart, because the whole course of your life flows out of it” (4:23). In the Bible the heart is the centre of a person, where thinking, choosing and loving begin.

Wisdom and Folly

Into the father’s teaching steps another voice. “Wisdom shouts out in the street; in the open squares she makes her voice heard” (1:20). In Hebrew the word for wisdom is feminine, and Proverbs pictures her as a woman, a prophet in the public square, calling to anyone who will listen. She is not hidden away for the few.

In chapter 8 she speaks of where she came from. Before the mountains were shaped, before there were oceans or springs, she was there. And when the LORD set the heavens in place and gave the sea its boundary, she was beside him:

I was right beside him, a master worker, and I was his delight day after day, always at play in his presence, playing over the whole world he had made, and delighting in the human race.

— Proverbs 8:30–31

This is poetry, not a lecture on how the world began. Its point is that wisdom is woven into creation itself. The world was made with wisdom, so to live wisely is to live with the grain of the world, and to live foolishly is to cut against it. Wisdom’s joy in creation spills over into delight in “the human race”.

Chapter 9 brings the opening poems to a close with two invitations. Wisdom has built her house on seven pillars, prepared a feast and sent out her servants. Across the way sits the woman Folly, loud and knowing nothing, at the door of her own house. Both call out in exactly the same words: “Whoever is naive, come in here!” (9:4, 16). Wisdom offers bread and wine and life. Folly offers stolen water, which “tastes sweet”, but her guests “lie deep in Sheol”. Every reader has to decide which house to enter.

How a proverb works

From chapter 10 the poems give way to sayings, most of them two lines long. Often the second line turns the first around with a “but”: “A wise son is his father’s joy, but a foolish son is a sorrow to his mother” (10:1). Sometimes it sharpens it, sometimes it adds a picture. “Like golden apples set in silver is a word spoken at just the right moment” (25:11). The sayings are compressed on purpose, to be turned over in the mind.

It matters that they are proverbs and not promises. A proverb says how things usually go in God’s world, not what must happen in every case. “Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not leave it” (22:6) is wise and true, but it is not a guarantee that every child of faithful parents will walk with God. Proverbs itself shows this by setting side by side two sayings that seem to contradict each other:

Do not answer fools on the terms of their folly, or you will become like them yourself. Answer fools as their folly deserves, or they will think themselves wise.

— Proverbs 26:4–5

Both are right, and the wise person is the one who can tell which fits the moment. Proverbs does not give you a rule book; it trains your judgement.

The book can also be funny. “As a door swings back and forth on its hinge, so the lazy one turns over in bed” (26:14). The lazy man will not go out because “There is a lion on the road!” (26:13). Agur marvels at things too wonderful to understand: an eagle in the sky, a snake on a rock, a ship at sea, “and the way a man and a young woman come together” (30:19).

Words, work, wealth and friends

Read through the sayings and certain subjects keep coming back.

  • Words. No subject is more common. “A gentle reply calms anger, but a hurtful word makes tempers flare” (15:1).
  • Work. “You lazy one, go and look at the ant; watch how it lives, and learn wisdom” (6:6). Diligence is honoured; idleness ends in a field overgrown with thorns (24:30–34).
  • Wealth and the poor. Proverbs commends honest gain and warns that riches cannot buy what matters: “Better to have little and fear the LORD than great riches with trouble” (15:16). Above all it insists that how you treat the poor is how you treat God.
  • Friendship. “A friend is loving through every season, and a brother is born to stand with you in trouble” (17:17). “As iron is sharpened against iron, so one person sharpens another” (27:17).
  • Pride and humility. “Pride comes first, then the crash; a haughty spirit, then the fall” (16:18). “The fear of the LORD teaches wisdom, and humility comes before honor” (15:33).

On the poor, one saying gathers up the book’s whole conviction:

Whoever oppresses the poor insults the One who made them, but kindness to the needy honors him.

— Proverbs 14:31

Our plans and God’s purpose

Proverbs is a practical book, full of advice about planning ahead, taking counsel and working hard. Yet it never lets the reader think that a well-made plan puts life under human control. Running through the sayings is a quiet confidence that God is at work in every outcome:

People plot their course in their minds, but it is the LORD who guides their steps.

— Proverbs 16:9

“People have many plans in their minds, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will prevail” (19:21). Even the toss of the lot is his: “The lot is tossed into the lap, but how it falls is decided by the LORD” (16:33). This is not a reason to stop planning, but to plan humbly, to “Hand over what you do to the LORD” (16:3), and to hold tomorrow loosely: “Do not brag about tomorrow; you have no idea what a single day will bring” (27:1).

Proverbs also knows that the wicked sometimes prosper for a while, and that the honest may stay poor. It says so in its “better” sayings: “Better a little gained honestly than a fortune made by injustice” (16:8). But it mostly leaves the hardest questions, why the righteous suffer and why everything seems to come to nothing, to the books that stand beside it, Job and Ecclesiastes. Together the three make up the wisdom books of the Old Testament, and each needs the others.

The capable wife

The book ends with a poem of twenty-two verses, each beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, a praise of wisdom from the first letter to the last. It opens with a question: “A capable wife, who can find her? She is worth far more than red coral” (31:10). She rises before dawn, buys a field, trades, provides for her household and opens her hand to the poor. “Strength and splendor clothe her, and she laughs at the time to come” (31:25).

Readers have heard this poem in more than one way. Many read it as the portrait of a real and admirable woman, and in Jewish homes it is sung at the table on the eve of the Sabbath in honour of the wife and mother. Others notice how closely she resembles Wisdom in chapters 1–9: she is worth more than red coral, as Wisdom is (3:15; 8:11), she speaks wisdom, and she is praised in the city gates where Wisdom called out. The book that began with Wisdom calling ends with Wisdom lived out in a home. The two readings belong together, and neither makes the poem a weight to lay on any one woman. Its last word is the book’s first:

Charm can deceive and beauty fades like a breath, but a woman who fears the LORD is the one to be praised.

— Proverbs 31:30

Proverbs and the New Testament

The apostles quote Proverbs as living Scripture. James and Peter both cite 3:34, which James gives as “God sets himself against the proud, but to the humble he gives grace” (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5). Hebrews 12:5–6 quotes the father’s words about the LORD’s discipline (3:11–12). Paul tells the Romans to feed a hungry enemy, in the words of 25:21–22 (Romans 12:20), and 2 Peter 2:22 calls 26:11 “The true proverb”.

More than that, the New Testament finds the wisdom of Proverbs fulfilled in a person. Jesus said of himself that “here is something greater than Solomon” (Matthew 12:42). Paul calls Christ “God’s power and God’s wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1:24), and says that in him “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge lie hidden” (Colossians 2:3). When John writes that the Word was with God in the beginning and that all things came into being through him, and when Colossians says that “all things are held together in him”, many readers hear an echo of Wisdom beside the Creator in Proverbs 8.

In the fourth century that chapter became the centre of a great argument. Arius pointed to 8:22, where the ancient Greek translation has Wisdom say that the Lord created her, as proof that the Son was a creature. Athanasius answered that the verse spoke of the Son taking flesh for our sake, not of his beginning, and that the Word through whom all things were made could not himself be made. Since then, Christians have generally read Wisdom in Proverbs 8 as pointing to Christ while denying that 8:22 makes him a creature; many modern readers take the chapter first as a poem about God’s wisdom, which the New Testament shows to have a human face.

How to read Proverbs

Proverbs is best read slowly and often. A few ways in:

  • A chapter a day. With thirty-one chapters, the book fits the library’s Proverbs in a Month plan exactly. On the fourteenth, read chapter 14.
  • Read chapters 1–9 first. They are the frame for everything else. Once you have heard the father, Wisdom and Folly, the short sayings make more sense.
  • Take one saying with you. From each day’s chapter, choose one proverb and carry it through the day.
  • Remember what kind of book it is. A proverb is a true word about how life usually goes under God, not a promise for every case. Let Job and Ecclesiastes keep it honest.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Proverbs is almost entirely poetry, so this edition prints each line on its own, as the Hebrew sets it out, and you will see the two halves of each saying stand one above the other. A few of its choices in Proverbs are worth knowing before you begin.

“The LORD.” When you see LORD in capital letters, it stands for God’s personal name, the four Hebrew letters YHWH, which this translation, like most English Bibles, follows long custom in printing as “the LORD”.

“The fear of the LORD.” The book’s motto keeps its familiar wording, “the fear of the LORD”. It means reverent awe that trusts and obeys, as 3:5–7 and 8:13 show, not dread.

“The naive.” The young person who is open to every influence, older Bibles’ “the simple”, is called “the naive”: “You naive people, how much longer will you love being naive?” (1:22). It is not an insult but a warning. The naive can still become wise, if they will listen.

“The woman who is not yours.” The woman of chapters 2, 5 and 7, older Bibles’ “strange woman”, is rendered by what she is: “the woman who is not yours to have, the stranger whose words are smooth and flattering” (2:16).

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Proverbs 1
fields.body_html:
The purpose of the proverbs

1These are the proverbs of Solomon, David’s son, king of Israel.
2They are for learning wisdom and discipline,
for grasping words of insight,
3for taking in the training that brings good sense:
righteousness, justice and fairness,
4for making the naive shrewd,
and giving the young knowledge and the ability to plan wisely.
5Let the wise listen and gain still more learning;
let those with understanding acquire skill to steer their way,
6so that they understand proverbs and figures of speech,
the sayings of the wise and their riddles.
7Knowledge begins with the fear of the LORD,
but fools treat wisdom and discipline with contempt.

Refuse the invitation of sinners

8My son, listen when your father corrects you,
and do not let go of what your mother teaches you.
9For they will be a lovely wreath on your head
and ornaments hanging around your neck.
10My son, if sinners try to lure you, do not go along with them.
11If they say, “Come with us;
let us lie in wait to shed blood;
let us set an ambush for the innocent, for no reason;
12let us gulp them down alive, as Sheol does,
whole, like people going down into the pit;
13we will come away with riches of every kind
and pack our houses with what we take;
14join your lot to ours;
there will be one purse for all of us,”
15my son, do not go down that road with them;
keep your feet off their path.
16For their feet race toward evil,
and they are in a hurry to kill.
17It is useless to spread a net
in full view of any bird.
18But it is their own blood they are waiting to shed;
it is their own lives they ambush.
19That is how it goes for all who grab at dishonest profit:
their profit costs them their lives.

Wisdom calls in the streets

20Wisdom shouts out in the street;
in the open squares she makes her voice heard.
21At the busiest corners, above the noise, she calls out;
at the city gates where people go in and out,
she makes her speech:
22“You naive people, how much longer will you love being naive?
How long will mockers enjoy their mocking,
and fools hate knowledge?
23Turn back when I rebuke you,
and I will pour out my heart to you
and make my words known to you.
24But since I called and you would not come,
since I held out my hand and no one took notice,
25since you brushed aside all my advice
and would have no part of my correction,
26so when ruin comes to you, I too will laugh;
when the thing you dread arrives, I will jeer,
27when terror sweeps over you like a storm
and ruin like a whirlwind,
when trouble and hardship close in on you.
28Then they will cry out to me, but I will give no answer;
they will search hard for me without finding me.
29All this because they hated knowledge,
and the fear of the LORD was not what they chose.
30They refused my advice
and treated every correction I gave with contempt.
31So they will eat what their own way of life has produced
and have more than enough of their own schemes.
32The naive turn away, and it kills them;
fools feel safe and at ease, and it destroys them.
33But anyone who listens to me will live securely,
at rest and free from the fear of harm.”
fields.summary: The proverbs of Solomon are given to teach wisdom, and the fear of God is where knowledge begins. A father warns his son not to join sinners, and Wisdom calls out in the streets to those who refuse to listen.

fields.title: Proverbs 2
fields.body_html:
Wisdom is worth the search

1My son, if you take hold of what I say
and hide my commands away like treasure,
2so that your ear is tuned to wisdom
and your heart leans toward understanding;
3if you truly cry out for insight
and raise your voice to call for understanding,
4if you go looking for it as you would for silver,
and hunt for it as for buried treasure,
5then you will come to see what the fear of the LORD is,
and you will discover what it is to know God.
6For it is the LORD who gives wisdom;
knowledge and understanding come from his mouth.
7He keeps sound wisdom in reserve for the upright;
he shields those who live with integrity,
8watching over the paths of justice
and protecting the way of those who are loyal to him.
9Then you will understand righteousness, justice and fairness,
and every good road to take.
10For wisdom will come into your heart,
and knowing will become a delight to you.
11foresight will stand guard over you,
and understanding will keep you safe,
12rescuing you from the road of evil,
from people whose speech twists the truth,
13who desert the honest road
to go walking down dark ways,
14who enjoy doing wrong
and celebrate the twisted ways of evil,
15people whose roads wind and twist,
who go astray at every turn.
16It will also rescue you from the woman who is not yours to have,
the stranger whose words are smooth and flattering,
17who has turned her back on the man she married when young,
and let the covenant of her God slip from her mind.
18Her house slides down into death,
and her paths end among the dead.
19None who go in to her ever come back,
nor do they reach the paths of life again.
20So you will go the way good people go
and stay on the paths of the righteous.
21For it is the upright who will live in the land,
and those with integrity who will remain there,
22but the wicked will be removed from the land,
and the treacherous will be uprooted from it.
fields.summary: If the son searches for wisdom like hidden treasure, he will understand the fear of God and be kept from evil men and from the adulterous woman.

fields.title: Proverbs 3
fields.body_html:
Keep my teaching

1My son, do not let my teaching slip from your memory;
hold my commands close in your heart,
2for they will lengthen your days, add years to your life,
and bring you peace.
3Never let loyal love and faithfulness leave you:
wear them like a necklace,
and engrave them on your heart as on a tablet,
4So you will find favor and be well thought of,
both by God and by people.

Trust God, not your own insight

5Trust the LORD with your whole heart,
and do not rely on your own insight.
6Keep him in mind in everything you do,
and he will clear a straight road ahead of you.
7Do not think of yourself as wise;
fear the LORD and keep away from evil.
8It will be medicine for your body
and fresh strength for your bones.
9Honor the LORD with what you own,
with the first and best of everything your land produces;
10then there will be more than enough to fill your barns,
and new wine will burst out of your vats.

The LORD’s discipline and the worth of wisdom

11My son, do not brush aside the discipline of the LORD,
or grow weary of his correction,
12for the LORD corrects the one he loves,
as a father corrects the son who is his joy.
13How blessed is the person who has found wisdom,
the one who has come by understanding,
14for what she earns you is worth more than silver,
and her return is better than gold.
15She is worth more than red coral;
nothing you long for comes close to her.
16She holds long life in her right hand,
and wealth and honor in her left.
17Her ways are delightful,
and every path she takes leads to peace.
18To those who take hold of her she is a tree of life;
whoever keeps a firm grip on her is called blessed.

Wisdom in creation and among neighbors

19It was with wisdom that the LORD set the earth on its foundations,
and with understanding that he fixed the heavens in place;
20by his knowledge the deep waters broke open,
and the clouds let the dew fall.
21My son, do not let these slip out of your sight;
hold on to sound wisdom and foresight,
22and they will be life to you
and a lovely ornament around your neck.
23Then your road will be safe to walk,
and your foot will not strike against anything.
24When you go to bed, you will have nothing to fear;
you will lie down and sleep soundly.
25You need not fear sudden terror,
or the storm that falls on the wicked when it comes,
26for the LORD will be the one you rely on,
and he will keep your foot from the snare.
27When you have it in your power to do good to those who are owed it,
do not hold it back.
28Do not tell your neighbor,
“Go away and come back; I will give it to you tomorrow,”
when you have it with you now.
29Do not plot harm against your neighbor,
who lives beside you and trusts you.
30Do not pick a fight for no reason
with someone who has done you no wrong.
31Do not be jealous of the violent,
and do not take up any of their ways,
32for the devious are hateful to the LORD,
but the upright are his close friends.
33The house of the wicked lies under the curse of the LORD,
but the home where the righteous live receives his blessing.
34Mockers he meets with mockery,
but to the humble he gives grace.
35Honor is what the wise inherit,
but fools are held up to disgrace.
fields.summary: The son is to trust God with his whole heart and not rely on his own insight, to honor God with his wealth and to accept God’s discipline. Wisdom is more precious than jewels.

fields.title: Proverbs 4
fields.body_html:
Get wisdom at any cost

1Listen, sons, to the correction a father gives;
pay attention, and you will gain understanding.
2What I am giving you is sound teaching;
do not walk away from my instruction.
3When I was a boy in my father’s house,
young and tender, my mother’s dearest child,
4he taught me and said to me,
“Hold on to my words with all your heart;
keep my commands and you will live.
5Get wisdom, get understanding;
do not forget what I have said, or turn away from it.
6Do not leave her, and she will watch over you;
love her, and she will protect you.
7This is where wisdom starts: get wisdom.
Spend all you have, if you must, to get understanding.
8Cherish her, and she will lift you up;
hold her close, and she will bring you honor.
9She will set a lovely wreath on your head
and present you with a glorious crown.”
10Listen, my son, and take in what I say,
and you will have many years of life.
11I have taught you the way of wisdom
and guided you along straight paths.
12When you walk, nothing will hem in your steps;
when you run, you will not trip.
13Grip discipline tightly and do not let it go;
guard it well, for it is your life.
14Do not step onto the road the wicked take,
or go marching along the way of evil people.
15Keep clear of it, and do not travel on it;
turn away from it and keep going.
16For they cannot sleep until they have done some harm;
they lie awake unless they have brought someone down.
17Wickedness is the bread they eat,
and violence the wine they drink.
18But the road the righteous walk is like the light at daybreak,
shining brighter and brighter until it is broad day.
19The way of the wicked is like deep darkness;
they do not even know what makes them fall.

Guard your heart

20My son, pay attention to what I say;
turn your ear to my words.
21Do not let them out of your sight;
keep them deep within your heart.
22To those who find them they are life,
and health for their whole body.
23More than anything you protect, protect your heart,
because the whole course of your life flows out of it.
24Rid yourself of a crooked mouth;
keep lying lips far away from you.
25Keep your eyes on what is in front of you,
and fix your gaze on the road ahead.
26Make the path for your feet level,
and every road you take will be firm.
27Do not veer off to either side;
keep your feet away from evil.
fields.summary: A father urges his sons to get wisdom above all else and to protect their hearts, for the whole course of life flows out of the heart. The path of the righteous grows brighter, while the way of the wicked is darkness.

fields.title: Proverbs 5
fields.body_html:
The bitter end of adultery

1My son, listen closely to the wisdom I have;
bend your ear to what I understand,
2so that you keep your foresight
and your lips guard what you know.
3For honey drips from the lips of the woman who is not yours,
and her talk is smoother than olive oil,
4but what she leaves you with is bitter as wormwood,
and it cuts like a two-edged sword.
5Her feet go down toward death;
her steps make straight for Sheol.
6She does not consider the road to life;
her ways drift, and she is unaware of it.

Keep away from her door

7So now, sons, hear me out,
and do not stray from the words I speak.
8Keep well away from her,
and do not even come near her front door,
9or you will hand over your strength to others
and your years to someone without mercy,
10and strangers will feed on your wealth,
and what you worked hard for will end up in an outsider’s house,
11and when it is all over you will groan,
your body wasted and your flesh used up,
12and you will say, “How I hated being corrected!
How my heart despised every warning!
13I paid no attention to what my teachers said;
I would not lend an ear to those who taught me.
14I came close to complete ruin,
there in front of the whole assembled community.”
15Draw your water from your own cistern,
the fresh streams from inside your own well.
16Why let your springs run out into the street,
and your streams flow through the town squares?
17Keep them for yourself alone,
with no strangers drinking beside you.
18May your spring be blessed;
find your joy in the woman you married when you were young,
19a lovely doe, a graceful mountain goat.
Let her breasts content you at every season,
and let her love carry you away always.
20Why, my son, let yourself be carried away by a woman who is not yours,
or take an outsider in your arms?
21For everything a person does is in plain view of the LORD,
and he weighs every path they take.
22Their own wrongdoing will catch the wicked,
and the ropes of their sin will tie them up.
23Such people die for lack of discipline,
carried away by their great folly.
fields.summary: The son is warned against the adulterous woman, whose ways lead to death, and urged to find joy in the wife of his youth.

fields.title: Proverbs 6
fields.body_html:
Get free from a rash pledge

1My son, if you have guaranteed a loan for your neighbor
and shaken hands on it for a stranger,
2the words of your mouth have snared you;
what you said has caught you.
3So, my son, do this and get yourself free,
since you have fallen into your neighbor’s power:
go and humble yourself, and keep pressing your neighbor.
4Give your eyes no sleep
and your eyelids no rest.
5Get yourself free like a gazelle from the hunter’s grip,
like a bird from the hand of the one who traps it.

Learn from the ant

6You lazy one, go and look at the ant;
watch how it lives, and learn wisdom.
7It has no chief, no overseer and no ruler,
8yet it gets its food ready in summer
and gathers its supplies at harvest time.
9Lazy one, how long will you stay lying there?
When will you rise from sleeping?
10“A bit more sleep, a bit more dozing,
a bit more lying with arms folded,”
11and poverty will be on you like a drifter on the road,
and need like a man with a shield.

The troublemaker

12A scoundrel, a troublemaker,
goes about with twisted speech,
13winking with the eye, shuffling the feet,
signaling with the fingers,
14with a heart full of deceit, always planning harm
and stirring up quarrels.
15So disaster will come on such a person suddenly,
and in a moment break them beyond healing.

Seven things the LORD hates

16Six things the LORD hates,
and seven he detests with his whole being:
17eyes that look down on others, a tongue that tells lies,
hands that spill innocent blood,
18a heart that works out wicked plans,
feet in a hurry to run to evil,
19a false witness who breathes out lies,
and one who sows quarrels among brothers and sisters.

Another man’s wife

20My son, hold on to your father’s command
and do not let go of what your mother teaches you.
21Keep them tied to your heart at all times;
wear them knotted around your neck.
22As you walk, it will lead you;
as you lie down, it will keep watch over you;
and when you wake, it will talk with you.
23For a command is a lamp and teaching is a light,
and the warnings that discipline brings are the road to life,
24to guard you from the evil woman
and the smooth tongue of the outsider.
25Do not let your heart crave her beauty,
and do not let her catch you with her glances,
26For a prostitute’s price may be only a loaf of bread,
but a married woman stalks a man’s whole life.

Playing with fire

27Can a man carry fire against his chest
and not set his clothes alight?
28Or can a man walk over live coals
and his feet not be burned?
29It is the same with the man who sleeps with his neighbor’s wife:
anyone who touches her will pay for it.
30People do not despise a thief who steals
to fill an empty stomach when he is starving,
31yet if he is caught he must pay back seven times over,
even if it takes everything in his house.
32But a man who commits adultery has no sense;
only someone bent on destroying himself would do it.
33Blows and disgrace will be his,
and his shame will never be erased.
34For jealousy makes a husband furious,
and when the day of revenge comes he will not hold back.
35He will accept no payment to settle it,
and no gift, however large, will satisfy him.
fields.summary: The son is warned against rash pledges and laziness, and told to learn from the ant. Seven things God hates are listed, and adultery is shown to be ruinous.

fields.title: Proverbs 7
fields.body_html:
The young man and the adulteress

1My son, hold on to what I say,
and keep my commands safe like treasure.
2Keep my commands and you will live;
guard my teaching as carefully as the pupil of your eye.
3Tie them around your fingers;
inscribe them on your heart as on a tablet.
4Tell wisdom, “You are my sister,”
and give understanding the name of dearest friend,
5so that they keep you from the woman who is not yours,
the outsider with her flattering words.
6Once, from the window of my house,
I looked down through the lattice,
7and among the naive I saw,
among the young men I noticed,
a youth with no sense,
8walking down the street near her corner,
stepping out along the road to her house,
9at dusk, as the day turned to evening,
as the black of night came on.
10Then out came a woman to meet him,
dressed as a prostitute, her mind full of schemes.
11She is loud and unruly;
her feet never stay at home.
12One moment she is out in the street,
the next in the squares,
waiting in ambush at every corner.
13She grabs him and kisses him,
and with a brazen face she tells him,
14“I had peace offerings to make,
and today I have kept my vows.
15That is why I came out looking for you;
I was eager to see you, and here you are!
16I have spread my couch with covers,
with colored sheets of Egyptian linen.
17I have scented my bed with myrrh,
aloes and cinnamon.
18Come, let us drink deep of love until morning
and take our pleasure in lovemaking.
19The man of the house is away;
he has gone on a long trip.
20He took a bag of money with him
and will not be home until the full moon.”
21With all her powers of persuasion she wins him over;
with her smooth talk she pushes him on.
22All at once he is following her,
like an ox on its way to be slaughtered,
like a fool in fetters on the way to punishment,
23until an arrow splits his liver;
like a bird rushing into a snare,
he has no idea it will cost him his life.

Her house is the road to death

24So now, sons, listen to me;
pay close attention to what I say.
25Do not let your heart drift toward her ways
or stray onto her paths,
26for she has brought down many victims,
and those she has killed are without number.
27Her house is the highway into Sheol,
sloping down to the rooms of death.
fields.summary: A young man without sense is led astray by an adulterous woman, going like an ox to the slaughter.

fields.title: Proverbs 8
fields.body_html:
Wisdom calls to everyone

1Listen! Is that not Wisdom calling,
Understanding raising her voice?
2On the high places by the road,
where the paths cross, she takes her stand;
3beside the gates where the town is entered,
at the doorways, she calls aloud:
4“To you, all people, I am calling;
my voice goes out to everyone on earth.
5You who are naive, learn to be shrewd;
you fools, get some sense.
6Listen, for what I say is worthy of a prince,
and right is what my lips bring out.
7For my mouth speaks the truth;
my lips cannot stand wickedness.
8Every word from my mouth is right;
there is nothing twisted or crooked in any of them.
9They are all plain to anyone with understanding,
and right to those who have found knowledge.
10Choose my discipline instead of silver,
and knowledge over the finest gold.
11For wisdom is worth more than red coral;
nothing you could want comes close to her.
12I, Wisdom, share my home with Prudence,
and I find knowledge and good planning.
13To fear the LORD is to hate evil.
Pride, arrogance, evil conduct and twisted talk are what I hate.
14Counsel and sound judgment belong to me;
I am Understanding, and I have strength.
15Through me kings rule,
and rulers make just laws.
16Through me princes govern,
and nobles, all who judge rightly.
17Those who love me I love in return,
and those who search hard for me will find me.
18Riches and honor are mine to give,
lasting wealth and righteousness.
19What I produce is better than gold, the purest gold,
and what I yield beats the finest silver.
20I walk on the road of righteousness,
right along the paths of justice,
21giving those who love me real wealth as their inheritance
and filling their storehouses.

Wisdom at the creation

22The LORD brought me into being as the first of his ways,
before his works of long ago.
23Long ages ago I was set in place, at the very first,
before the earth began.
24Before there were any oceans I was born,
before there were springs full of water.
25Before the mountains were set on their foundations,
before the hills, I was born,
26before he had made the land and the open country,
or the first specks of the world’s soil.
27I was there when he set the heavens in place,
when he drew a circle on the face of the deep,
28when he fixed the clouds overhead
and made the springs of the deep flow strong,
29when he gave the sea its boundary
so that the waters would not go beyond his command,
when he laid out the foundations of the earth,
30I was right beside him, a master worker,
and I was his delight day after day,
always at play in his presence,
31playing over the whole world he had made,
and delighting in the human race.

Listen and live

32So now, children, listen to me:
how blessed are those who keep to my ways!
33Listen to correction and become wise; do not brush it aside.
34How blessed is the one who hears me,
who keeps watch at my doors every day
and waits by my doorposts.
35For the one who finds me has found life
and wins the favor of the LORD.
36But whoever fails to find me does violence to their own life;
all who hate me are in love with death.”
fields.summary: Wisdom calls out, declaring her worth above silver and gold. She was with God before the world was made, rejoicing in creation, and whoever finds her finds life.

fields.title: Proverbs 9
fields.body_html:
Wisdom’s feast

1Wisdom has built a house for herself
and shaped seven pillars for it.
2She has slaughtered her animals for the feast, mixed her wine
and set her table.
3She has sent her young women out with the invitation;
she calls from the high places of the town:
4“Whoever is naive, come in here!”
To anyone who lacks sense she says,
5“Come, have some of my food
and taste the wine I have blended.
6Leave your naive ways behind and live;
walk straight down the road of understanding.
7Correct a mocker and you will be insulted;
rebuke the wicked and you will get hurt.
8Do not rebuke a mocker, or you will be hated;
rebuke the wise, and you will be loved.
9Give advice to the wise and they will grow wiser still;
teach the righteous and they will add to what they know.

Wisdom and the woman Folly

10Wisdom starts with the fear of the LORD,
and to know the Holy One is understanding.
11For through me your days will be many,
and the years of your life will grow.
12If you are wise, your wisdom will benefit you;
if you mock, the cost is yours alone.”
13The woman Folly makes a lot of noise;
she is gullible and has no knowledge.
14She takes her seat in her doorway,
on a chair up on the town’s heights,
15calling to those who pass by,
who are going straight along on their way:
16“Whoever is naive, come in here!”
And to anyone who lacks sense she says,
17“Water that is stolen tastes sweet,
and food eaten where no one sees is a delight.”
18But those who turn in have no idea that the dead are in that house,
that her guests lie deep in Sheol.
fields.summary: Wisdom builds her house and invites the simple to her feast, while Folly calls to them from her door; her guests are in the depths of the grave.

fields.title: Proverbs 10
fields.body_html:
The proverbs of Solomon

1The proverbs of Solomon.
A wise son is his father’s joy,
but a foolish son is a sorrow to his mother.
2Wealth gained by wickedness does no good in the end,
but righteousness rescues from death.
3The LORD will not leave the righteous to starve,
but he pushes away what the wicked crave.
4A slack hand leads to poverty,
but hard-working hands bring wealth.
5A son who gathers the crops in summer is wise;
a son who sleeps through harvest brings disgrace.
6The righteous wear blessings like a crown,
but violence lies hidden behind the words of the wicked.
7The righteous are remembered with blessing,
but the name of the wicked decays.
8The wise in heart accept instruction,
but a fool who keeps talking will come to ruin.
9Whoever lives honestly walks without fear,
but the one who takes crooked roads will be exposed.
10Someone who winks with the eye causes trouble,
and a fool who keeps talking will come to ruin.
11What the righteous say is a spring of life,
but behind the words of the wicked lies violence.
12Hatred starts fights,
but love draws a veil over every wrong.
13Wisdom is found on the lips of a person of understanding,
but the rod is for the back of one with no sense.
14The wise keep knowledge in store,
but a fool’s mouth invites ruin.
15A rich person’s wealth is a fortified city;
poverty is what ruins the poor.
16What the righteous earn leads to life;
what the wicked gain leads to sin.
17Whoever holds on to discipline is on the road to life,
but whoever rejects correction leads others astray.
18Hiding hatred makes for lying lips,
and spreading slander makes a fool.
19Where there are many words, wrongdoing is never far away,
but whoever holds back their words is wise.
20The tongue of the righteous is pure silver;
the heart of the wicked is worth very little.
21The words of the righteous nourish many,
but fools die for lack of sense.
22It is the blessing of the LORD that makes rich,
and hard work adds nothing to it.
23Doing wrong is a game to a fool,
but a person of understanding delights in wisdom.
24What the wicked dread is what will happen to them,
but what the righteous long for will be given to them.
25When the whirlwind has passed through, the wicked are gone,
but the righteous have a foundation that lasts forever.
26Like vinegar on the teeth or smoke in the eyes
is a lazy messenger to those who send him.
27The fear of the LORD lengthens life,
but the years of the wicked are cut off early.
28What the righteous hope for ends in joy,
but the hopes of the wicked come to nothing.
29For those with integrity the way of the LORD is a refuge,
but for evildoers it is ruin.
30The righteous will never be moved,
but the wicked will not remain in the land.
31Wisdom grows from the mouth of the righteous like fruit,
but a twisted tongue will be cut out.
32The righteous know how to say what is pleasing,
but the wicked speak only what is twisted.
fields.summary: The proverbs of Solomon contrast the wise and the foolish, the righteous and the wicked, the diligent and the lazy, and words that bring life with words that bring ruin.

fields.title: Proverbs 11
fields.body_html:
1The LORD detests dishonest scales,
but an honest weight pleases him.
2When pride arrives, disgrace follows close behind,
but the humble have wisdom.
3The upright are guided by their integrity,
but the treacherous are ruined by their own deceit.
4Riches are of no use on the day of wrath,
but righteousness rescues from death.
5The righteousness of the blameless clears their road,
but the wicked are brought down by their own wickedness.
6The righteousness of the upright sets them free,
but the treacherous are trapped by their own greed.
7When the wicked die, their hope dies with them,
and all they expected from their strength is gone.
8The righteous are rescued from trouble,
and the wicked fall into it instead.
9With their words the godless bring ruin on their neighbors,
but the righteous escape by knowing better.
10When the righteous do well, the whole town celebrates;
when the wicked perish, there are cheers.
11A city is built up by the blessing of the upright,
but the talk of the wicked tears it down.
12Whoever belittles a neighbor has no sense,
but a person of understanding holds their tongue.
13A gossip goes around giving away secrets,
but a trustworthy person keeps a confidence.
14Without wise direction a nation falls,
but with many advisers comes victory.
15Whoever guarantees a stranger’s debt will be badly hurt,
but whoever refuses to shake on such deals is safe.
16A gracious woman gains honor,
and ruthless men gain only riches.
17People who are kind do themselves good,
but the cruel bring harm on their own bodies.
18The wicked earn pay that does not last,
but whoever sows righteousness reaps a sure reward.
19Real righteousness leads to life,
but chasing after evil leads to death.
20The LORD detests those with twisted hearts,
but people of integrity are his delight.
21Be sure of this: the wicked will not escape punishment,
but the children of the righteous will go free.
22A lovely woman who has no sense
is a gold ring stuck in a pig’s snout.
23What the righteous long for ends only in good,
but what the wicked hope for ends in wrath.
24One person gives freely and gains even more;
another holds back what should be given and ends up in need.
25A generous person will prosper,
and whoever refreshes others will be refreshed.
26People curse the one who hoards grain,
but they bless the one who sells it.
27Whoever works hard for what is good finds favor,
but trouble comes to anyone who looks for it.
28Those who put their trust in riches will fall,
but the righteous will flourish like green leaves.
29Whoever brings trouble on their family will inherit nothing but wind,
and the fool will end up serving the wise.
30What the righteous produce is a tree of life,
and whoever wins people over is wise.
31If even the righteous are paid what they are due on earth,
how much more will the wicked and sinners be!
fields.summary: The proverbs contrast honesty and deceit, pride and humility, generosity and greed; the generous will prosper.

fields.title: Proverbs 12
fields.body_html:
1To love discipline is to love knowledge;
to hate correction is plain stupidity.
2A good person wins favor from the LORD,
but he condemns the one who plots evil.
3No one is made secure by wickedness,
but the roots of the righteous cannot be dislodged.
4A capable wife is a crown on her husband’s head,
but a wife who disgraces him is decay in his bones.
5The plans of the righteous are fair,
but the advice of the wicked is full of deceit.
6When the wicked speak, they are setting an ambush to kill,
but what the upright say rescues them.
7The wicked are overthrown and gone,
but the house of the righteous will stand firm.
8People are praised for their good sense,
but the one with a twisted mind is held in contempt.
9Better to be a nobody with a servant
than to put on airs and have nothing to eat.
10The righteous take care of their animals,
but even the kindness of the wicked is cruel.
11Those who work their land will have plenty to eat,
but those who chase fantasies have no sense.
12The wicked want what evil people have caught,
but the root of the righteous bears fruit.
13The wicked are trapped by their sinful talk,
but the righteous get out of trouble.
14People are filled with good things by the fruit of their words,
and the work of their hands comes back to them.
15Fools think their own way is right,
but the wise listen to advice.
16A fool shows annoyance at once,
but a prudent person overlooks an insult.
17An honest witness tells what is right,
but a false witness tells lies.
18Thoughtless words cut like a sword,
but what the wise say heals.
19Truthful words endure forever,
but a lie is over in the blink of an eye.
20There is deceit in the hearts of those who plot evil,
but joy for those who work for peace.
21No real harm comes to the righteous,
but the wicked are full of trouble.
22The LORD detests lying lips,
but people who keep faith are his delight.
23Sensible people keep what they know to themselves,
but the minds of fools blurt out folly.
24Hard workers will end up in charge,
but the lazy will be made to work for others.
25Worry weighs down the heart,
but a kind word lifts it up.
26The righteous give their friends good direction,
but the road the wicked take leads them astray.
27The lazy never cook what they catch,
but the diligent value what they have.
28On the road of righteousness there is life;
along that path there is no death.
fields.summary: The proverbs speak of discipline, truthful lips, kind words and diligent work.

fields.title: Proverbs 13
fields.body_html:
1A wise son takes in his father’s correction,
but a mocker will not listen to a warning.
2People enjoy good things from the fruit of their words,
but the treacherous hunger for violence.
3Those who watch what they say protect their lives,
but those who talk carelessly come to ruin.
4The lazy want and want but get nothing,
while the diligent are fully satisfied.
5The righteous hate lies,
but the wicked bring disgust and disgrace.
6Righteousness protects the person of integrity,
but wickedness brings down the sinner.
7Some pretend to be rich but have nothing;
others pretend to be poor but have great wealth.
8The rich may have to pay a ransom for their lives,
but the poor never even hear a threat.
9The light of the righteous burns bright,
but the wicked have a lamp that will be snuffed out.
10Arrogance only stirs up fights,
but those who take advice are wise.
11Money that comes easily soon dwindles,
but whoever gathers it bit by bit makes it grow.
12When hope keeps being put off, the heart grows sick,
but a longing fulfilled is a tree of life.
13Whoever scorns instruction will pay the price,
but whoever respects a command will be rewarded.
14What the wise teach is a spring of life,
steering people away from the traps of death.
15Good sense wins goodwill,
but the way of the treacherous is rough going.
16The prudent act with knowledge,
but fools put their folly on display.
17An unreliable messenger lands in trouble,
but a trustworthy envoy brings healing.
18Poverty and disgrace come to the one who ignores discipline,
but whoever accepts correction is honored.
19A wish come true is sweet to the soul,
but fools hate to turn away from evil.
20Spend time with the wise and you will grow wise;
keep company with fools and you will get hurt.
21Trouble chases sinners,
but the righteous are rewarded with good things.
22A good person leaves an inheritance to their grandchildren,
but the wealth of a sinner ends up with the righteous.
23The fields of the poor may produce plenty of food,
but injustice sweeps it away.
24Whoever holds back the rod hates their son,
but the one who loves him is quick to discipline him.
25The righteous have enough to eat,
but the stomachs of the wicked go empty.
fields.summary: The proverbs speak of guarding one’s words, hope deferred and fulfilled, the company of the wise, and the discipline of children.

fields.title: Proverbs 14
fields.body_html:
1A wise woman builds up her home,
but a foolish one pulls it down with her own hands.
2Whoever lives uprightly fears the LORD,
but whoever goes crooked ways despises him.
3A fool’s talk is a rod for his own back, the fruit of his pride,
but the words of the wise keep them safe.
4Without oxen the feeding trough stays clean,
but it takes a strong ox to bring a big harvest.
5An honest witness does not deceive,
but a false witness pours out lies.
6A mocker goes looking for wisdom and comes up empty,
but a person of understanding learns with ease.
7Stay away from a fool,
for you will not hear knowledge from his lips.
8The prudent are wise because they think about where they are going,
but the folly of fools is self-deception.
9Fools make light of guilt,
but among the upright there is goodwill.
10Each heart knows its own sorrow,
and no outsider can share its joy.
11The house of the wicked will be wiped out,
but the tent of the upright will thrive.
12There is a road that looks right to a person,
but at the end of it is death.
13Even while laughing the heart may ache,
and joy can end in sorrow.
14The faithless will get their fill of their own ways,
and the good will be rewarded for theirs.
15The naive believe everything they hear,
but the prudent watch where they are going.
16The wise are careful and turn away from evil,
but a fool is reckless and overconfident.
17Someone with a short temper acts foolishly,
and the one who schemes is hated.
18The naive end up with folly as their inheritance,
but the prudent are crowned with knowledge.
19In the end the evil bow low to the good,
and the wicked come begging at the doors of the righteous.
20The poor are shunned even by their neighbors,
but the rich have plenty of friends.
21To look down on a neighbor is a sin,
but how blessed is the one who is kind to the humble.
22Surely those who plot evil go astray,
but those who plan good find loyal love and faithfulness.
23All hard work brings a profit,
but mere talk leads only to poverty.
24Wealth is a crown for the wise,
but the folly of fools brings only folly.
25A truthful witness saves lives,
but one who pours out lies is a traitor.
26Whoever fears the LORD has a secure fortress,
and their children will have a refuge.
27The fear of the LORD is a spring of life,
steering people away from the traps of death.
28A king’s glory is in having many people;
without people a ruler is ruined.
29Patience shows great understanding,
but a quick temper puts folly on display.
30A calm heart gives life to the body,
but envy is decay in the bones.
31Whoever oppresses the poor insults the One who made them,
but kindness to the needy honors him.
32The wicked are brought down by their own evil,
but the righteous have a refuge even in death.
33Wisdom is at home in the heart of the discerning,
and even among fools it makes itself known.
34Righteousness lifts a nation up,
but sin brings disgrace on any people.
35A king shows favor to a wise servant,
but his anger falls on one who disgraces him.
fields.summary: The proverbs contrast the wise and the foolish, warn that a road that looks right can end in death, and teach that the fear of God is a fountain of life.

fields.title: Proverbs 15
fields.body_html:
1A gentle reply calms anger,
but a hurtful word makes tempers flare.
2The wise use knowledge well when they speak,
but fools spout nonsense.
3There is no place the LORD does not see;
his eyes watch both the evil and the good.
4Kind words are a tree of life,
but a twisted tongue crushes the spirit.
5A fool rejects his father’s discipline,
but whoever accepts correction shows good sense.
6The home of the righteous holds great treasure,
but the earnings of the wicked bring trouble.
7The wise spread knowledge with their words,
but the minds of fools do no such thing.
8The LORD detests the sacrifices of the wicked,
but the prayers of the upright are his delight.
9The way the wicked live is detestable to the LORD,
but he loves anyone who strives after righteousness.
10Harsh discipline waits for whoever leaves the right path;
whoever hates correction will die.
11If Sheol and Destruction are in full view of the LORD,
how much more are human hearts!
12Mockers resent being corrected;
they will not go to the wise for advice.
13A happy heart lights up the face,
but heartache crushes the spirit.
14A discerning mind looks for knowledge,
but fools feed on folly.
15Every day is hard for the afflicted,
but a cheerful heart has a constant feast.
16Better to have little and fear the LORD
than great riches with trouble.
17Better a plate of greens where there is love
than a fattened calf served with hatred.
18A hot-tempered person starts fights,
but one who is patient calms a quarrel.
19For the lazy, the road is a thorn hedge,
but for the upright it is a smooth highway.
20A wise son makes his father glad,
but only a fool would scorn his mother.
21Folly delights a person with no sense,
but someone with understanding keeps to a straight path.
22Plans go wrong for lack of advice,
but with many advisers they succeed.
23Giving a good answer is a joy,
and a word at the right time, how good it is!
24For the wise, the road of life climbs upward,
away from Sheol beneath.
25The LORD tears the house of the proud to the ground,
but he keeps the widow’s boundary stones in place.
26The LORD detests evil plans,
but kind words are pure in his sight.
27Those greedy for dishonest gain bring trouble on their families,
but those who hate bribes will live.
28The righteous think before they answer,
but the wicked spew out evil.
29The LORD keeps far from the wicked,
but he listens to the prayers of the righteous.
30A bright look brings joy to the heart,
and good news puts strength in the bones.
31Whoever listens to correction that gives life
will be at home among the wise.
32Those who ignore discipline despise themselves,
but those who heed correction gain understanding.
33The fear of the LORD teaches wisdom,
and humility comes before honor.
fields.summary: A gentle reply calms anger; the proverbs teach that God sees everything and that a cheerful heart and good counsel bring life.

fields.title: Proverbs 16
fields.body_html:
1People make the plans in their minds,
but the right answer comes from the LORD.
2People think all their ways are pure,
but the LORD weighs the motives.
3Hand over what you do to the LORD,
and your plans will stand firm.
4The LORD has made everything for its own end,
even the wicked for the day of disaster.
5The LORD detests all the proud of heart;
be sure of it, they will not escape punishment.
6Loyal love and faithfulness make amends for wrong,
and through the fear of the LORD people turn away from evil.
7When the LORD is pleased with how someone lives,
he makes even their enemies make peace with them.
8Better a little gained honestly
than a fortune made by injustice.
9People plot their course in their minds,
but it is the LORD who guides their steps.
10A king’s words are like an oracle;
when he gives judgment, his mouth should not go wrong.
11Honest scales and balances belong to the LORD;
every weight in the bag is his concern.
12Kings detest wrongdoing,
for a throne is made secure by righteousness.
13Kings take pleasure in honest speech;
they value the one who speaks what is right.
14A king’s anger is a messenger of death,
but a wise person will calm it.
15When the king’s face shines with favor, there is life,
and his goodwill is like a rain cloud in spring.
16How much better to gain wisdom than gold,
to choose understanding rather than silver!
17The highway of the upright avoids evil;
whoever watches their step protects their life.
18Pride comes first, then the crash;
a haughty spirit, then the fall.
19Better to be humble and live among the lowly
than to share the spoils with the proud.
20Whoever heeds instruction will prosper,
and how blessed is the one who trusts in the LORD!
21The wise in heart are known for their discernment,
and pleasant words make teaching more persuasive.
22Good sense is a spring of life to those who have it,
but folly is the punishment of fools.
23A wise heart guides the mouth
and makes the lips more persuasive.
24Kind words are a honeycomb,
sweet to taste and health for the body.
25There is a road that seems right to a person,
but where it ends is death.
26A worker’s hunger works for him;
his mouth drives him on.
27A scoundrel digs up trouble,
and their talk is like a scorching fire.
28A twisted person stirs up conflict,
and a gossip separates close friends.
29A violent person lures a neighbor
and leads them down a bad road.
30Someone who winks is plotting something twisted;
someone who purses the lips has already done harm.
31Gray hair is a glorious crown,
won by living a righteous life.
32Patience is worth more than a warrior’s strength,
and self-control more than conquering a city.
33The lot is tossed into the lap,
but how it falls is decided by the LORD.
fields.summary: People make plans, but God directs their steps; pride comes before the fall, and patience is better than strength.

fields.title: Proverbs 17
fields.body_html:
1Better a dry crust eaten in peace
than a house full of feasting and quarrels.
2A servant with good sense will end up over a son who brings disgrace,
and will get a share of the inheritance with the brothers.
3Silver is tried in the crucible and gold in the furnace,
but it is the LORD who tests the heart.
4Evildoers pay attention to wicked talk;
liars listen eagerly to malicious words.
5Whoever mocks the poor insults the One who made them;
whoever gloats over disaster will not escape punishment.
6Grandchildren are the crown of the elderly,
and children take pride in their parents.
7Eloquent words do not suit a fool;
still less do lies suit a leader.
8A bribe seems like a lucky charm to the one who gives it;
wherever he turns, it works.
9Whoever forgives a wrong builds up love,
but whoever keeps bringing it up drives friends apart.
10A single rebuke does more for a person of understanding
than a hundred lashes for a fool.
11The wicked are bent only on rebellion,
so a merciless messenger will be sent against them.
12Facing a mother bear robbed of her cubs is safer
than facing a fool in the middle of his folly.
13If anyone pays back good with evil,
evil will never leave their house.
14Starting a quarrel is like breaching a dam;
so drop it before the fight bursts out.
15Acquitting the guilty and condemning the innocent:
the LORD detests them both.
16What use is money in a fool’s hand to buy wisdom,
when he has no mind to learn?
17A friend is loving through every season,
and a brother is born to stand with you in trouble.
18Only someone with no sense shakes hands on a pledge
and puts up security for a neighbor.
19Whoever loves quarrels loves sin;
whoever builds a high gate invites ruin.
20A crooked heart finds nothing good,
and a deceitful tongue lands in trouble.
21To raise a fool is to grieve;
the father of a fool knows no joy.
22A cheerful heart heals like medicine,
but a broken spirit saps the body’s strength.
23The wicked accept a bribe slipped from a pocket
to twist the course of justice.
24The discerning keep wisdom in view,
but a fool’s eyes wander to the ends of the earth.
25A son who is a fool is a sorrow to his father
and a bitter grief to the mother who bore him.
26It is wrong to fine the innocent,
or to flog officials for their honesty.
27Whoever holds back words has knowledge,
and someone with a steady spirit has understanding.
28Even fools are thought wise if they keep quiet;
if they close their lips, they seem discerning.
fields.summary: The proverbs commend peace, faithful friendship and a cheerful heart, and warn against strife and bribes.

fields.title: Proverbs 18
fields.body_html:
1Whoever keeps apart from others pursues selfish desires
and lashes out at all good sense.
2A fool takes no pleasure in understanding,
only in airing his own opinions.
3With wickedness comes contempt,
and with shame comes disgrace.
4A person’s words can be deep waters,
and the spring of wisdom a rushing stream.
5It is not good to favor the guilty
or to deny justice to the innocent.
6A fool’s lips lead him into quarrels,
and his mouth asks for a beating.
7A fool’s mouth is his undoing,
and his lips trap his own life.
8Gossip is like tasty bites of food;
it goes all the way down inside.
9Anyone who is slack in their work
is close kin to someone who destroys.
10The name of the LORD is a fortress tower;
the righteous run to it and are kept safe on high.
11The rich think their wealth is a fortified city,
a high wall around them, but only in their imagination.
12A proud heart goes before a fall,
and humility comes before honor.
13To answer before listening
is foolish and shameful.
14The human spirit can hold up under illness,
but who can bear a broken spirit?
15A discerning mind gains knowledge,
and the wise listen out for more.
16A gift opens doors for the giver
and brings him into the presence of the great.
17The first to state a case sounds right,
until the other side comes and asks questions.
18Casting lots settles disputes
and keeps powerful opponents apart.
19A brother wronged is harder to win back than a fortified city;
quarrels are like the bolted gates of a castle.
20People will be filled by the fruit of their words;
they will be satisfied by the harvest of their lips.
21The tongue has the power of life and death,
and those who love to talk will eat what it produces.
22The man who finds a wife finds something good
and receives favor from the LORD.
23The poor must beg for mercy;
the rich can afford to answer roughly.
24Someone with many companions may still be ruined,
but some friends stay closer than a brother.
fields.summary: The proverbs warn against isolation, foolish talk and gossip; the name of God is a fortress tower, and the tongue has the power of life and death.

fields.title: Proverbs 19
fields.body_html:
1Better to be poor and live with integrity
than to be a fool with a lying tongue.
2Zeal without knowledge is not good;
whoever rushes ahead misses the way.
3People ruin their lives by their own folly,
and then their hearts rage against the LORD.
4Wealth brings many friends,
but the poor lose even the friends they have.
5A false witness will not escape punishment,
and one who pours out lies will not get away.
6Many try to win a ruler’s favor,
and everyone is a friend to the one who gives gifts.
7All the relatives of the poor shun them;
how much more do their friends keep away!
The poor go after them with pleas, but they are gone.
8To gain sense is to love yourself;
to hold on to understanding is to prosper.
9A false witness will not escape punishment,
and one who pours out lies will perish.

10Luxury does not suit a fool;
still less should a servant rule over princes.
11Good sense makes a person patient,
and it is to their credit to overlook an offense.
12A king in a rage roars like a lion,
but his goodwill falls like dew on the grass.
13A foolish son ruins his father,
and a quarrelsome wife is like a leaky roof that never stops dripping.
14House and wealth are inherited from parents,
but a sensible wife is from the LORD.
15Laziness brings on deep sleep,
and an idle person will go hungry.
16Whoever keeps the commandment preserves their life,
but whoever is careless about how they live will die.
17Whoever is kind to the poor is lending to the LORD,
and he will pay them back for what they have done.
18Discipline your son while there is still hope;
do not make yourself responsible for his death.
19A hot-tempered person must pay the penalty;
if you bail them out, you will only have to do it again.
20Listen to advice and accept correction,
so that in the end you will be wise.
21People have many plans in their minds,
but it is the purpose of the LORD that will prevail.
22What people want in a person is loyalty;
better to be poor than a liar.
23The fear of the LORD leads to life;
whoever has it rests content, untouched by trouble.
24The lazy bury their hand in the dish
and will not even lift it back to their mouth.
25Flog a mocker, and the naive will learn a lesson;
correct the discerning, and they will gain knowledge.
26A son who robs his father and drives out his mother
brings shame and disgrace.
27My son, if you stop listening to correction,
you will stray from the words of knowledge.
28A corrupt witness makes a mockery of justice,
and the wicked swallow evil whole.
29Penalties stand ready for mockers,
and the rod for fools’ backs.
fields.summary: The proverbs speak of poverty and integrity, of kindness to the poor as a loan to God, and of discipline and God’s purpose that will stand.

fields.title: Proverbs 20
fields.body_html:
1Wine makes people mock and strong drink makes them rowdy;
no one who reels under them is wise.
2A king’s fury is like a lion’s roar;
anyone who angers him puts their own life at risk.
3Staying out of a fight brings honor,
but every fool is ready to burst into one.
4The lazy will not plow in the cold season;
at harvest they look for a crop and find nothing.
5A person’s real intentions lie deep, like water in a well,
but someone with understanding can bring them up.
6Plenty of people speak of their own loyalty,
but who can find one who is really faithful?
7The righteous live with integrity;
how blessed are their children after them!
8A king seated on his judgment throne
sifts out every evil with a look.
9Who can say, “My heart is pure;
I am cleansed of my sin”?
10Two sets of weights, two sizes of measure:
the LORD detests them both.
11Even the young show who they are by what they do,
whether their conduct is pure and right.
12The ear that hears and the eye that sees:
the LORD is the maker of both.
13Do not love sleep, or you will end up poor;
keep your eyes open, and you will have food to spare.
14“No good, no good,” says the buyer,
then goes off and boasts about the bargain.
15There is gold, and jewels in abundance,
but lips that speak knowledge are a rarer treasure.
16Take the coat of one who puts up security for a stranger;
if they do it for a foreign woman, hold it as a pledge.
17Bread won by deceit tastes sweet at first,
but afterward it fills the mouth with grit.
18Make your plans firm by taking counsel,
and wage war only with wise guidance.
19A gossip goes around giving away secrets,
so have nothing to do with a person who cannot keep their mouth shut.
20Those who curse their father or mother
will have their lamp snuffed out in deep darkness.
21An inheritance grabbed too early
will not be blessed in the end.
22Do not say, “I will pay back this wrong!”
Wait for the LORD, and he will rescue you.
23The LORD detests two sets of weights;
cheating scales are wrong.
24The LORD directs each person’s steps,
so how can anyone make sense of where they are going?
25It is a trap to declare something holy without thinking
and to have second thoughts only after making the vow.
26A wise king sifts the wicked like grain
and rolls the threshing wheel over them.
27The human spirit is the lamp of the LORD,
shining into every hidden part of a person.
28Loyal love and faithfulness keep a king safe;
by loyal love he makes his throne secure.
29Young men take pride in their strength;
the old wear gray hair as their honor.
30Blows that wound scour away evil,
and beatings cleanse the inner self.
fields.summary: The proverbs warn against wine, strife and laziness, and teach that God weighs the heart and that the human spirit is God’s lamp.

fields.title: Proverbs 21
fields.body_html:
1A king’s heart is like streams of water in the hand of the LORD,
who directs it wherever he pleases.
2People think every road they take is right,
but the LORD weighs the heart.
3The LORD would rather see people do what is right and just
than offer sacrifice.
4Proud eyes and an arrogant heart,
the lamp that lights the way of the wicked, are sin.
5The plans of the diligent bring nothing but gain,
but all who rush in haste come to nothing but need.
6Riches gained by a lying tongue are a mist that drifts away,
and those who seek them seek death.
7The wicked are swept away by their own violence,
since they will not do what is just.
8The path of the guilty is twisted,
but the conduct of the pure is straight.
9It is better to live up in a corner of the rooftop
than to share a home with a wife who quarrels.
10The wicked hunger for evil;
their neighbors find no mercy from them.
11When a mocker is punished, the naive learn wisdom;
when the wise are taught, they take in knowledge.
12The Righteous One watches over the house of the wicked
and throws the wicked down to ruin.
13Whoever stops their ears to the cry of the poor
will also call out one day and get no answer.
14A gift given in secret calms anger,
and a bribe tucked in the cloak quiets fierce rage.
15When justice is done, the righteous rejoice,
but evildoers are filled with dread.
16Whoever strays from the path of good sense
will come to rest in the company of the dead.
17Those who love pleasure will end up poor;
those who love wine and fine oil will never be rich.
18The wicked serve as ransom for the righteous,
and the treacherous go in place of the upright.
19It is better to live in the wilderness
than with a wife who quarrels and frets.
20Valuable treasure and oil are stored in the home of the wise,
but a fool gulps it all down.
21Whoever chases after what is right and loyal love
finds life, vindication, and honor.
22A wise person can scale a city held by warriors
and pull down the stronghold they relied on.
23Whoever watches their mouth and tongue
keeps themselves out of trouble.
24The proud and haughty earn the name of mocker;
they act with boundless arrogance.
25The lazy one’s cravings will be the death of them,
because their hands refuse to work.
26All day long the lazy only crave more,
but the righteous give without holding back.
27The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable,
and all the more when it is offered with evil intent.
28A false witness will perish,
but one who listens carefully will speak with lasting effect.
29The wicked put on a bold face,
but the upright give thought to the way they go.
30No wisdom, no understanding,
no plan can stand against the LORD.

31People ready the horse for the day of battle,
yet the victory belongs to the LORD.
