fields.summary: God directs the heart of the king, and doing what is right pleases God more than sacrifice; the proverbs warn against pride, laziness and quarrels.

fields.title: Proverbs 22
fields.body_html:
1A good reputation is worth choosing over great wealth;
being well regarded is better than silver and gold.
2Rich and poor alike share one thing:
the LORD is the maker of them all.
3Sensible people see danger coming and take cover,
but the naive walk straight into it and suffer for it.
4Humility and the fear of the LORD bring their reward:
riches, honor, and life.
5Thorns and traps lie on the road of the crooked;
whoever values their life stays well away from them.
6Start children off on the way they should go,
and even when they are old they will not leave it.
7The rich lord it over the poor,
and whoever borrows becomes the lender’s slave.
8Those who sow injustice will reap disaster,
and the rod they swing in anger will fail.
9Generous people will be blessed,
because they share their food with the poor.
10Throw out the mocker, and conflict goes too;
quarrels and insults come to an end.
11Whoever loves a pure heart
and speaks with grace will have the king for a friend.
12The eyes of the LORD keep watch over knowledge,
but he brings the words of the faithless to nothing.
13The lazy one says, “A lion is out there!
I will be murdered in the open street!”
14The talk of forbidden women is a deep pit;
anyone the LORD is angry with will fall into it.
15Foolishness is tied fast to a child’s heart,
but the rod of discipline will drive it far away.
16Whoever exploits the poor to get rich,
or hands gifts to the rich, will only end up in need.
17Bend your ear and hear what the wise have said,
and set your mind on the knowledge I give,
18for it is good to keep them deep inside you,
every one of them ready on your lips.
19I am teaching you today, yes, you,
so that you will put your trust in the LORD.
20Have I not written you thirty sayings
full of counsel and knowledge,
21to teach you what is right and reliable,
so that you can bring back a true answer to those who send you?

Thirty sayings of the wise

22Do not rob the poor just because they are poor,
and do not crush the needy in court,
23for the LORD will take up their cause
and take the life of those who plunder them.
24Do not make friends with someone hot-tempered,
and do not keep company with those quick to rage,
25or you may learn their ways
and set a trap for your own life.
26Do not be one of those who shake hands on a pledge
and guarantee other people’s loans.
27If you cannot pay,
why let them take even the bed you sleep on?
28Do not shift the old boundary stone
that your ancestors put in place.
29Do you see someone who is skilled at their work?
They will serve kings, not people of no account.
fields.summary: A good reputation is worth more than great wealth, and children should be started off on the way they should go. The words of the wise begin, warning against robbing the poor.

fields.title: Proverbs 23
fields.body_html:
1When you are seated at a ruler’s table,
take careful note of what is in front of you,
2and if you have a big appetite,
hold a knife to your own throat.
3Do not long for the ruler’s fine dishes,
for that food is deceptive.
4Do not wear yourself out to get rich;
have the sense to stop.
5Cast a glance at wealth, and it is gone;
it grows wings
and flies off to the sky like an eagle.

6Do not eat at the table of a stingy host,
and do not long for their fine food,
7Such people are always counting the cost.
“Eat and drink!” they say to you,
but their heart is not with you.
8You will throw up the little you have eaten
and squander your gracious words.
9Do not talk to a fool,
who will only scorn your wise words.
10Do not shift an ancient boundary marker
or encroach on the fields of orphans,
11for their Defender is strong,
and he will argue their cause against you.
12Set your mind on instruction
and your ears on words of knowledge.
13Do not hold back correction from a child;
if you punish them with the rod, they will not die.
14Punish them with the rod yourself,
and you will save their life from Sheol.
15My son, if you have a wise heart,
then I myself will be glad at heart.
16I will be glad to the depths of my being
when I hear you speak what is right.
17Do not let your heart envy sinners;
instead, live in the fear of the LORD all day long.
18Surely there is a future for you,
and your hope will not be cut off.
19Listen, my son, and become wise;
set your heart straight on the way.
20Do not keep company with heavy drinkers of wine
or with those who stuff themselves with meat,
21For drunkards and gluttons will end up poor,
and their drowsiness will dress them in rags.
22Listen to the father who gave you life,
and do not look down on your mother when she is old.
23Buy the truth and never sell it;
get wisdom, discipline, and understanding.
24The father of a righteous son will be full of joy;
a man who has a wise son will delight in him.
25Let your father and mother be glad;
let her who gave birth to you rejoice.
26Give me your heart, my son,
and let your eyes watch my ways.
27A prostitute is a deep pit;
a foreign woman is a narrow well.
28She lies in wait like a robber
and makes many men unfaithful.
29Who has trouble? Who has misery? Who is always fighting? Who is always complaining?
Who has bruises for no reason?
Who has bloodshot eyes?
30Those who stay up late over wine,
who go looking for spiced drinks.
31Do not gaze at the red wine
as it gleams in the cup
and slides down so easily.
32But at the last it bites like a snake
and strikes like a viper.
33Your eyes will see strange sights,
and your mind will say confused and twisted things.
34You will be like someone sleeping in the middle of the sea,
like someone lying at the top of a ship’s mast.
35“They hit me,” you will say, “but I was not hurt;
they beat me, but I did not feel it.
When will I wake up?
I will go and look for another drink.”
fields.summary: The sayings of the wise warn against overeating, chasing wealth and drunkenness, and urge children to listen to their parents.

fields.title: Proverbs 24
fields.body_html:
1Do not be envious of evil people
or wish you could be with them,
2because their minds are set on violence
and their talk is all about causing harm.
3A house is built through wisdom
and made secure through understanding;
4by knowledge its rooms are filled
with every kind of rich and lovely treasure.
5Wise people have great power,
and those with knowledge grow ever stronger.
6You should wage war with careful guidance;
victory comes from having many advisers.
7Wisdom is out of a fool’s reach;
at the city gate, where matters are decided,
the fool has nothing to say.
8Whoever plots to do evil
will be known as a schemer.
9Foolish scheming is sin,
and people detest a mocker.
10If you give up when times are hard,
how little strength you have!
11Rescue those being dragged off to death;
hold back those who are stumbling toward slaughter.
12If you say, “But we knew nothing about this,”
does not the one who weighs hearts see the truth?
The one who watches over your life knows it well,
and he will repay each person for what they have done.
13My son, eat honey, because it is good;
honey from the comb tastes sweet.
14Know that wisdom is like that for your soul:
find it, and you will have a future,
and your hope will not fail.

15Do not lie in ambush like a criminal at the home of a righteous person;
do not raid the place where they live.
16For the righteous may fall seven times and still get up again,
but the wicked are brought down by calamity.
17When your enemy falls, do not celebrate;
when they trip up, do not let your heart be glad,
18or the LORD will see it and be displeased,
and turn his anger away from them.
19Do not get upset about those who do evil
or be envious of the wicked,
20for evil people have no future;
the lamp of the wicked will go out.
21Fear the LORD and the king, my son,
and have nothing to do with those who want to overturn things,
22for disaster will strike them without warning,
and who can tell what ruin the LORD and the king can bring?

More sayings of the wise

23These also are sayings of the wise:
It is not right to show favoritism in a court case.
24Whoever tells the guilty, “You are innocent,” will be cursed by peoples
and condemned by nations.
25But those who convict the guilty will be well thought of,
and a rich blessing will come on them.
26To give a straight answer
is to kiss the lips.
27Get your work outside in order and your fields ready first;
after that, build your house.

28Do not testify against your neighbor without good reason,
or use your lips to mislead.
29Do not say, “I will treat them the way they treated me;
I will pay them back for what they did.”
30I walked past the field of someone lazy,
past the vineyard of someone with no sense,
31and I saw thorns had sprung up everywhere,
weeds had covered the ground,
and its stone wall lay in ruins.
32I looked at it and thought it over;
I saw it and learned a lesson:
33a bit more sleep, a bit more dozing,
a bit more lying with arms folded,
34and poverty will be on you like a drifter on the road,
and need like a man with a shield.
fields.summary: The sayings of the wise warn against envying the wicked, urge rescuing those led to death, and describe the field of the lazy.

fields.title: Proverbs 25
fields.body_html:
Proverbs copied by Hezekiah’s officials

1These too are proverbs of Solomon, collected and copied by the officials of Hezekiah, king of Judah.
2God is honored for keeping things hidden,
and kings are honored for getting to the bottom of things.
3As high as the heavens and as deep as the earth,
so the mind of a king is beyond anyone’s probing.
4Take the impurities out of silver,
and the smith has material for a fine vessel.
5Take the wicked out of the king’s presence,
and his throne will be made secure by justice.
6Do not promote yourself in the king’s presence
or take your stand among the great,
7for it is better to be told, “Come up here,”
than to be sent lower in front of a noble
you have seen with your own eyes.
8Do not rush to bring a case to court,
for what will you do at the end
if your neighbor proves you wrong and shames you?
9Argue your case with your neighbor directly,
and do not give away someone else’s secret,
10or whoever hears it will shame you,
and your bad reputation will never go away.
11Like golden apples set in silver
is a word spoken at just the right moment.
12A wise person’s rebuke, given to an ear that listens,
is a gold earring, a jewel of the finest gold.
13Like the coolness of snow in harvest time
is a reliable messenger to those who send them;
they refresh the spirit of their masters.

14Like clouds and wind that bring no rain
is someone who brags about gifts they never give.
15With patience you can win over a ruler,
and a gentle tongue can break bone.
16If you find honey, eat only what you need,
or you will have too much and throw it up.
17Do not set foot in your neighbor’s house too often,
or they will get tired of you and come to dislike you.
18Anyone who gives false testimony against a neighbor
is a war club, a sword, a sharpened arrow.
19Like a bad tooth or a lame foot
is trust in a traitor when trouble comes.
20Like taking someone’s coat away on a cold day, or like pouring vinegar on soda,
is singing cheerful songs to a heavy heart.

21If your enemy is hungry, give them something to eat;
if they are thirsty, give them water to drink,
22for you will be heaping burning coals on their head,
and the LORD will reward you.
23As a north wind brings rain,
so a gossiping tongue brings angry looks.
24It is better to live up in a corner of the rooftop
than to share a home with a wife who quarrels.
25Like cold water to someone worn out and thirsty
is good news from far away.
26When the righteous give way before the wicked,
it is a trampled spring, a fouled well.
27Eating honey to excess does no good,
and seeking honor for yourself brings no honor.
28Someone without self-control
is a city breached, left with no walls.
fields.summary: More proverbs of Solomon, copied by the officials of Hezekiah, speak of kings, patience and kindness to enemies.

fields.title: Proverbs 26
fields.body_html:
1Snow does not belong in summer, nor rain at harvest time,
and honor does not belong with a fool.
2Like a sparrow flitting about or a swallow darting past,
an undeserved curse flies back to the one who spoke it.
3The horse needs a whip, the donkey a bridle,
and the backs of fools a rod.
4Do not answer fools on the terms of their folly,
or you will become like them yourself.
5Answer fools as their folly deserves,
or they will think themselves wise.
6Whoever sends a message by a fool
cuts off their own feet and drinks down trouble.
7Like the useless legs of someone who is lame
is a proverb in the mouth of fools.
8Giving honor to a fool
is like tying a stone into a sling.
9Like a thorn branch in the hand of a drunk
is a proverb in the mouth of fools.
10Like an archer who shoots at anyone
is the one who hires a fool or any stranger passing by.
11As a dog goes back to its vomit,
so fools return to their foolishness.
12Do you see people who are wise in their own eyes?
A fool has more hope than they do.
13The lazy one says, “There is a lion on the road!
A lion loose in the streets!”
14As a door swings back and forth on its hinge,
so the lazy one turns over in bed.
15The lazy bury their hand in the dish
and are too tired to lift it back to their mouth.
16The lazy think they are wiser
than seven people who can give a sensible answer.
17Like someone who seizes a stray dog by the ears
is a passerby who gets worked up
over a quarrel that is none of their business.
18Like a maniac who hurls flaming darts, arrows and death,
19so is anyone who tricks a neighbor
and then says, “I was only joking!”
20When the wood runs out, the fire goes out;
when there is no gossip, quarrels die down.
21As charcoal feeds embers and wood feeds fire,
so a quarrelsome person keeps conflict burning.

22Gossip is like tasty bites of food;
it goes all the way down inside.
23Like a coat of silver dross over a clay pot
are warm words that hide an evil heart.
24People who hate disguise it with their words,
while inside they harbor deceit.
25When they speak graciously, do not believe them,
for seven detestable things fill their hearts.
26Hatred may hide behind deceit,
but their wickedness will be exposed before the whole community.
27Whoever digs a pit will fall into it;
whoever starts a stone rolling will have it roll back on them.
28A lying tongue hates the people it hurts,
and flattering words bring ruin.
fields.summary: The proverbs describe the fool, the lazy person, the gossip and the deceiver.

fields.title: Proverbs 27
fields.body_html:
1Do not brag about tomorrow;
you have no idea what a single day will bring.
2Let someone else praise you, not your own mouth;
an outsider, not your own lips.
3Stone is heavy and sand is a load,
but the aggravation a fool causes weighs more than both.
4Rage is cruel and anger overwhelming,
but who can hold out against jealousy?
5An open rebuke is better
than love that stays hidden.
6A friend’s wounds can be trusted,
but an enemy’s kisses come in plenty.
7One who is full turns up their nose even at honey,
but to the hungry anything bitter tastes sweet.
8Like a bird that wanders from its nest
is anyone who wanders from home.
9Scented oil and incense delight the heart;
a friend’s sincere counsel is just as sweet.
10Never walk away from your own friend or from your father’s friend;
and when trouble comes,
you need not run to your brother’s house.
Better a neighbor close by than a brother far away.
11My son, become wise and make my heart glad,
so that I have a reply for anyone who taunts me.
12The sensible see trouble coming and take cover;
the naive keep going and pay for it.
13Take the garment of anyone who guarantees a stranger’s debt;
hold it as security if they do it for a foreign woman.
14Whoever blesses a neighbor with a loud voice at the crack of dawn
will have it counted as a curse.
15A quarrelsome wife
is like the endless drip of a leaking roof on a rainy day.
16Trying to restrain her is like trying to hold back the wind
or grip oil in your hand.
17As iron is sharpened against iron,
so one person sharpens another.
18Those who care for a fig tree will enjoy its figs,
and those who look after their master will receive honor.
19As water reflects a face,
so the heart reflects the person.
20Sheol and Destruction are never full,
and human eyes are never satisfied.
21The crucible tests silver and the furnace gold,
and praise tests a person.
22Even if you grind fools in a mortar with a pestle along with the grain,
you will not get their folly out of them.

Look after your flocks

23Know how your flocks are doing,
and keep your mind on your herds,
24for riches do not last forever,
and a crown does not pass down through every generation.
25When the hay is cut and the new growth shows,
and the grass of the hills is brought in,
26the lambs will give you clothing,
and the goats will buy a field.
27There will be goats’ milk enough for your food
and your household’s food,
and to keep your servant girls alive.
fields.summary: The proverbs warn against boasting about tomorrow and speak of faithful friends and careful work.

fields.title: Proverbs 28
fields.body_html:
1The wicked run away when nobody is chasing them,
but the righteous stand as bold as a lion.
2When a land rebels, it has one ruler after another,
but a person of understanding and knowledge keeps order lasting.
3A poor man who exploits the poor
is like a beating rain that leaves no crops behind.
4People who abandon God’s instruction speak well of the wicked,
but those who keep it stand up against them.

5Evil people cannot grasp what justice is,
but those who seek the LORD understand it fully.
6It is better to be poor and live with integrity
than to be rich and two-faced in all you do.
7A son who keeps instruction shows good sense,
but one who runs with gluttons disgraces his father.
8Whoever grows rich by charging interest and taking a cut
is only storing it up for someone who will be generous to the poor.
9If anyone refuses to listen to God’s instruction,
even their prayer is detestable.
10Whoever lures the upright into an evil path
will fall into their own pit,
but the blameless will receive good things.
11The rich may think they are wise,
but a poor person with insight sees right through them.
12When the righteous win, there is great celebration,
but when the wicked come to power, people go into hiding.
13Whoever hides their sins will not succeed,
but whoever admits them and turns away from them will receive mercy.
14How blessed is the one who is always reverent,
but whoever hardens their heart will fall into disaster.
15Like a roaring lion or a bear on the attack
is a wicked ruler over helpless people.
16A ruler without sense is a harsh oppressor,
but one who hates dishonest gain will reign long.

17Someone tormented by guilt for shedding blood will be a fugitive until death;
let no one stand in their way.
18Whoever lives with integrity will be kept safe,
but anyone who is double-dealing will suddenly fall.
19Those who farm their land will have food in plenty,
but those who chase fantasies will have poverty in plenty.
20A faithful person will be richly blessed,
but one who rushes to get rich will not escape punishment.
21Favoritism is never right,
yet some will do wrong for a mere scrap of bread.
22A stingy person is in a rush to get rich,
not knowing that poverty is on its way.
23In the end, a person who corrects someone will be more appreciated
than one who flatters.
24Whoever robs their father or mother
and says, “There is nothing wrong with that,”
is no better than a vandal.
25Greedy people stir up conflict,
but whoever trusts in the LORD will prosper.
26Whoever trusts their own mind is a fool,
but whoever walks in wisdom will be kept safe.
27Whoever gives to the poor will lack nothing,
but whoever looks away from them will receive many curses.
28When the wicked rise to power, people go into hiding,
but when the wicked are destroyed, the righteous flourish.
fields.summary: The proverbs contrast the righteous and the wicked, and teach that whoever confesses sin will find mercy.

fields.title: Proverbs 29
fields.body_html:
1Whoever is warned again and again yet stays stubborn
will be broken in a moment, past all remedy.
2When the righteous grow in number, the people are glad;
when the wicked rule, the people groan.
3A man who loves wisdom gives his father joy,
but one who spends his time with prostitutes squanders his wealth.
4By justice a king gives a country stability,
but one who is greedy for levies brings it to ruin.
5Whoever flatters a neighbor
is laying a net for that neighbor’s feet.
6An evil person is caught by his own wrongdoing,
but the righteous sing and rejoice.
7The righteous care about justice for the poor,
but the wicked have no such concern.
8Mockers set a city in an uproar,
but the wise calm its anger.
9When a wise person takes a fool to court,
the fool rages or laughs, and there is no peace.
10Bloodthirsty people hate those who are blameless,
but the upright care for their lives.
11Fools vent all their anger,
but the wise quietly hold it back.
12If a ruler pays attention to lies,
all his officials will become wicked.
13The poor and those who oppress them meet on common ground:
the LORD gives both of them the light of their eyes.
14When a king judges the poor fairly,
his throne will stand secure for all time.
15Discipline and correction give wisdom,
but a child left to do as he pleases disgraces his mother.
16When the wicked multiply, so does sin,
but the righteous will see them fall.
17Discipline your son, and he will give you peace of mind;
he will bring delight to your heart.

18Where there is no prophetic revelation, a people throws off all restraint;
but how blessed are those who keep God’s instruction!
19A servant cannot be corrected by words alone;
even if he understands, he will not respond.
20Do you see someone who speaks without thinking?
A fool has more hope than that person.
21Pamper a servant from childhood,
and in the end you will have trouble.
22An angry person stirs up conflict,
and a hot-tempered one commits many sins.
23Pride brings a person down,
but the humble in spirit gain honor.
24Whoever is a thief’s partner is their own enemy;
they hear the curse put on witnesses and say nothing.
25Fear of what people may do is a trap,
but whoever trusts in the LORD is kept safe.
26Many seek an audience with a ruler,
but it is from the LORD that people receive justice.
27The righteous detest the unjust,
and the wicked detest those whose way is straight.
fields.summary: The proverbs speak of correction, justice and the poor, and teach that whoever trusts in God will be safe.

fields.title: Proverbs 30
fields.body_html:
The words of Agur

1The sayings of Agur son of Jakeh, an oracle. This man declares to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal:
2I am surely the most ignorant of all people;
I lack ordinary human understanding.
3I have not learned wisdom,
nor do I have knowledge of the Holy One.
4Who has climbed up to heaven and come back down? Who has caught the wind in the palms of his hands? Who has bundled the waters in a cloak?
Who has fixed all the boundaries of the earth?
What is his name, and the name of his son? Tell me, if you know!
5Every word God speaks is proven true;
he is a shield to all who take refuge in him.
6Do not add anything to his words,
or he will correct you and show you to be a liar.

7I ask you for two things;
grant them to me before I die:
8Keep falsehood and lies far away from me;
give me neither poverty nor wealth,
but feed me with the bread I need each day,
9so that I do not have too much and disown you, asking,
“Who is the LORD?”
or have too little and steal,
and so bring disgrace on my God’s name.

10Do not speak against a servant to his master,
or the servant will call down a curse on you, and you will be found guilty.
11There are people who curse their fathers
and never speak well of their mothers.
12There are people who think they are clean,
yet their filth has never been washed away.
13There are people whose eyes are so haughty,
whose glances are full of scorn!
14There are people whose teeth are swords and whose jaws are set with knives,
to devour the afflicted off the earth
and the needy from the human race.

15The leech has two daughters, both called “Give!” Three things can never be filled;
four never say, “Enough!”:
16Sheol, the barren womb,
land that never has its fill of water,
and fire that never says, “Enough!”
17The eye that sneers at a father and scorns to obey a mother
will be pecked out by the ravens of the valley
and eaten by young vultures.

18There are three things that amaze me,
four that are beyond my understanding:
19An eagle making its way through the sky, a snake gliding over a rock,
a ship finding its way across the open sea,
and the way a man and a young woman come together.
20This is how an adulteress behaves:
she eats, wipes her mouth,
and says, “I did no wrong.”

21The earth shakes under three things;
there are four it cannot endure:
22a servant who becomes king,
a fool who has more than enough to eat,
23an unloved woman who finally gets a husband,
and a servant girl who takes her mistress’s place.

24On earth there are four small creatures
that are wiser than the wise:
25ants are a people without strength,
yet they store up their food in summer;
26rock badgers are a feeble folk,
yet they set up house among the crags;
27locusts have no king,
yet they all march out in ordered ranks;
28a lizard can be caught in the hand,
yet it lives in kings’ palaces.

29There are three things that move with dignity,
four that have a stately walk:
30the lion, strongest among the animals,
which retreats from nothing;
31the strutting rooster, the he-goat,
and a king at the head of his troops.
32If you have played the fool by putting yourself forward,
or if you have been scheming,
put your hand over your mouth!
33For as churning milk produces butter,
and pressing the nose produces blood,
so pressing anger produces a quarrel.
fields.summary: Agur speaks of the limits of human wisdom and asks for neither poverty nor riches, and lists sets of wonders and warnings.

fields.title: Proverbs 31
fields.body_html:
The words of King Lemuel

1The words of King Lemuel, an oracle that his mother taught him:
2“What shall I say, my son? What, child of my womb?
What, son of my vows?
3Do not pour out your strength on women,
nor your life on what brings kings to ruin.
4It is not for kings, Lemuel,
not for kings to drink wine,
nor for rulers to crave strong drink,
5or they will drink, forget the law,
and bend justice against everyone who suffers.
6Give strong drink to someone who is dying,
and wine to those whose hearts are bitter.
7Let them drink and forget their poverty
and remember their misery no more.
8Open your mouth for those who have no voice,
for the cause of all who are left to perish.
9Speak out and judge rightly;
take up the case of the poor and the needy.”

The capable wife

10A capable wife, who can find her?
She is worth far more than red coral.
11Her husband trusts her completely;
he never runs short of gain.
12She is good to him, never harmful,
as long as she lives.
13She looks for wool and flax
and works gladly with her hands.
14She is like a trader’s ships,
bringing her food from far away.
15She gets up while it is still dark
to provide food for her household
and a share for her servant girls.
16She looks over a field and buys it;
with what she has earned she plants a vineyard.
17She wraps herself in strength like a belt,
and her arms are firm for the work.
18She sees that her business turns a good profit;
her lamp stays lit at night.
19She reaches her hands to the distaff,
and her fingers hold the spindle.
20Her hand is open to the poor;
she reaches out to help the needy.
21Snow holds no fear for her when she thinks of her household,
for every one of them is dressed in scarlet.
22She makes her own bedspreads;
her clothing is fine linen and purple.
23Her husband is respected at the city gates,
where he takes his seat with the elders of the land.
24She makes linen garments and sells them;
she supplies sashes to the traders.
25Strength and splendor clothe her,
and she laughs at the time to come.
26Her words are wise,
and the teaching she gives is full of loyal love.
27She keeps a close watch on all that goes on in her house;
she never eats food she has not worked for.
28Her children rise and speak of her as blessed;
her husband too gives her praise:
29“Many women have shown strength and worth,
but you rise above them all.”
30Charm can deceive and beauty fades like a breath,
but a woman who fears the LORD is the one to be praised.
31Give her a share of what her hands have produced,
and let her deeds bring her praise at the city gates.
fields.summary: King Lemuel’s mother teaches him to defend the poor and needy. The book ends with a poem about a capable wife, whose worth is far above jewels and who fears God.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Who has climbed up to heaven and come back down? Who has caught the wind in the palms of his hands? Who has bundled the waters in a cloak? Who has fixed all the boundaries of the earth? What is his name, and the name of his son? Tell me, if you know!

— Proverbs 30:4

Near the end of a book full of confident advice comes a man who admits he does not know. Agur says he is “the most ignorant of all people” and has not learned “knowledge of the Holy One”. Then he asks the questions above, the oldest questions there are: who holds the wind, who set the bounds of the earth, what is his name? The book that has taught so much about how to live stops to confess that the source of all wisdom is beyond us, and must be given if it is to be known.

Agur’s answer is not more cleverness, but trust in what God has said: “Every word God speaks is proven true; he is a shield to all who take refuge in him” (30:5). Wisdom begins, and ends, with the fear of the LORD.

The question the book leaves with you

Proverbs is a book of choices. On every page two ways open up, the wise and the foolish, the righteous and the wicked, the diligent and the lazy, and the sayings describe where each one leads. At the end of the opening poems stand two houses, Wisdom’s and Folly’s, and from both doors the same call goes out to the same people: “Whoever is naive, come in here!” The question Proverbs leaves is simply which house you will enter, and whether you will keep coming back to Wisdom’s door.

That is not a choice made once. The book was meant to be read again and again, a little at a time, so that its sayings wear into the mind the way water wears a path in stone. A chapter a day is a good way to do it: in a month you will have read the whole book.

Where Proverbs points

Agur asked for the name of the one who holds the wind, “and the name of his son”. Christians have never been able to read that question without thinking of the answer the New Testament gives. Jesus taught as the wise teach, in sayings and parables, and the ancient Greek translation often used for mashal the word from which “parable” comes. He spoke of himself as “something greater than Solomon”. He invited the weary to come to him and learn, as Wisdom invites the naive to her table: “Come to me, all of you who are worn out with work and weighed down with burdens, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

Paul goes further. Christ, he says, “has become God’s wisdom for us, which means our righteousness, our holiness and our redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30). The wisdom that delighted beside the Creator and called out in the streets has come close enough to touch. And James adds a promise for anyone who reads Proverbs and feels how far short they fall: “If any of you is short of wisdom, ask God, who gives to everyone with an open hand and without scolding, and it will be given to you” (James 1:5).

Where to go from here

Preachers and teachers have mined Proverbs for practical wisdom for as long as there has been a church, and some of the best of that work is in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On the book’s purpose and its opening call (Proverbs 1). Alexander Maclaren’s sermon A Young Man’s Best Counsellor, on 1:1–19; and the chapter “The Holy Spirit in the Book of Proverbs” in A. B. Simpson’s The Holy Spirit, or Power from on High, Part I, which begins with Wisdom calling in the streets.
  • On guarding the heart (Proverbs 4:23). Maclaren’s Keeping and Kept, which sets the command to keep the heart beside the promise that God keeps us.
  • On Wisdom in Proverbs 8. Athanasius’s Against the Arians, whose second discourse works through 8:22 and its context at length.
  • On friendship, courage and drifting. Charles H. Spurgeon’s A Faithful Friend (18:24), R. A. Torrey’s Heroes and Cowards (29:25), and A. W. Tozer’s Causes of Backsliding (14:14).
  • On humility under God’s hand (Proverbs 16:19). Thomas Boston’s The Crook in the Lot, whose fourth part takes the saying that it is better to be humble among the lowly.
  • On wisdom for every day. Hannah Whitall Smith’s chapter “Proverbs: Guidance” in Old Testament Types and Teachings; and Spurgeon’s John Ploughman’s Talk, proverb-wisdom in plain country speech on idleness, debt, gossip and home.
  • Ochorus Originals. Growing in Wisdom, a guide for students built on the sayings of Proverbs; Clothed with Strength and Dignity, for women, which takes its title from 31:25 and returns to the capable wife throughout; and, for reading aloud with children, Tell Me the Story – Book 9: Songs and Wise Words, with chapters on the ant, a gentle answer and a friend who sticks close.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Proverbs in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

But the best next step is simply to begin again at chapter 1, and to read on a chapter a day. Wisdom is still standing at the gates, and she still makes the same promise:

For the one who finds me has found life and wins the favor of the LORD.

— Proverbs 8:35
